Let f be a step function on the interval [a, b]. Then f can be written as a finite linear combination of indicator functions of intervals:

f(x) = ∑_{i=1}^n c_i \chi_{I_i}(x)

where I_i are disjoint intervals and c_i are constants.

For each interval I_i, we can define a partition P_i of I_i into n_i subintervals, where n_i is the number of subintervals in I_i. Let P be the union of all P_i.

Then, for any partition P, we have:

∫_a^b f(x) dx = ∑_{i=1}^n c_i \int_{I_i} f(x) dx

= ∑_{i=1}^n c_i \sum_{j=1}^{n_i} f(x_j) \Delta x_j

where x_j are the endpoints of the subintervals in P_i and \Delta x_j are the lengths of the subintervals.

Since f is a step function, f(x_j) is constant for each j. Therefore, the sum ∑_{j=1}^{n_i} f(x_j) \Delta x_j is equal to the length of the interval I_i.

Thus, we have:

∫_a^b f(x) dx = ∑_{i=1}^n c_i \Delta x_i

where \Delta x_i is the length of the interval I_i.

This shows that f is Riemann Integrable, since the integral is a finite sum of constants.

Note that this proof assumes that the step function f is defined on a closed interval [a, b]. If f is defined on an open interval (a, b), then the proof is similar, but we need to use a different partition P that includes the endpoints a and b.
